one_liner: Research code for the SPIRE 2024 wavelet-forest paper: per-block SDSL Huffman wavelet trees instead of one global tree.
what_it_does: Splits a byte text into fixed-size blocks and builds one sdsl::wt_huff per block (stored as std::vector<sdsl::wt_huff<>>), then answers access(i) by indexing forest[i / block][i % block]. There is no library or API: the repo is three standalone programs (a random 8 MB byte-file generator, a builder that writes a global wt_huff and a 1 MiB-block forest, and an access timer) with placeholder file paths that must be edited before use. Only access is implemented; rank and select over the forest are not written.
how_it_is_fast: Wavelet forest (block-partitioned wavelet tree, as used in fixed-block compression boosting): each block's tree has small bitvectors, so a root-to-leaf access descent stays inside one small region of memory instead of touching log(sigma) far-apart bitvectors of a global tree. Search-result snippets of the paper put it as a wavelet-tree descent usually causing about 4 cache misses where a forest may cause one. The effect needs texts much larger than the last-level cache.
when_to_use: As a reference for reproducing or extending the 'Another Virtue of Wavelet Forests' experiments (access on byte alphabets, uncompressed bitvectors).
When you already use SDSL wt_huff for access-heavy queries on multi-GB byte texts and want a few-dozen-line sketch of the block-partitioned alternative to re-implement.
Large alphabets (hex, ASCII) where the README reports the forest most often ahead; block sizes around 0.5 MB are the README's suggested starting point.
when_not_to_use: As a library: there is no header, no API, no rank/select, no tests, and every program has hard-coded placeholder paths.
When you need numbers to justify the switch: the repo has none and its timing program is not a fair comparison (see gotchas).
Small texts that fit in cache (the generator's default is only 8 MB), or binary/DNA-sized alphabets, where the README itself reports little or no gain.
GPL-incompatible projects: the LICENSE is GPL-3.0 despite the README calling it permissive.
If you want a maintained fast wavelet structure: QWT (C++ or Rust) and faster-minuter's wt_fbb are complete libraries with rank/select.

integration.dependencies: sdsl-lite (fetched at HEAD via FetchContent), libdivsufsort 2.0.1, malloc_count v0.7.1, CLI11 v1.9.0 (included but unused), optional OpenMP
integration.platforms: not documented; Linux and macOS OpenMP paths in CMakeLists.txt
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the forest is a std::vector of sdsl::wt_huff, so per-block access uses the SDSL API, but global positions must be split by the caller and no global rank/select is provided

gotchas: The build is broken as checked in: the root CMakeLists.txt calls add_executable(wavelet_forest main.cpp) and likewise for randomFileGenerator.cpp and wavelet_engine.cpp, but those files live in src/ and there is no src/CMakeLists.txt, so configuration should fail on missing sources. The README's bin/gen_text, build_wt, build_wf and bench_access tools and CSV output do not exist.

Inconsistent block size: wavelet_engine.cpp builds the forest with 1 MiB (1,048,576-symbol) blocks while main.cpp looks it up with block_size = 10,000,000, so forest[idx / 10000000][idx % 10000000] indexes past the end of a 1 MiB block (undefined behaviour, wrong answers) unless the user edits one of them.

Off-by-one in the query generator: std::uniform_int_distribution<size_t>(0, size) is inclusive, so a query can hit position wt.size(), one past the end. Queries are seeded from std::random_device, so runs are not repeatable.

Unfair timing in main.cpp: the wavelet-tree loop discards wt[i] (the compiler may drop the work), while the forest loop prints every result to std::cout inside the timed region; only 10,000 queries, one run, and no build type or -O flags set in CMakeLists.txt.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it only to study or reproduce the wavelet-forest locality idea; for a usable fast wavelet structure, QWT (C++ quad-wavelet-tree or Rust qwt) has numbers about 2x over SDSL and full access/rank/select, and faster-minuter's wt_fbb is the maintained fixed-block-boosting wavelet tree with the same block-partitioning idea.
verified_claims_summary: No measurements are reachable: the README states qualitatively that the forest often beats an SDSL Huffman-shaped wavelet tree on access for ASCII and hex alphabets with uncompressed bitvectors, best near 0.5 MB blocks, citing the SPIRE 2024 paper (arXiv 2308.07809, blocked here); no compiler, flags or hardware are given, and the repo's own timer cannot reproduce a fair comparison.
status_note: Stale (last commit 2025-08-29, 1 star, 0 issues), GPL-3.0 research code that does not build as checked in; treat it as a paper companion, not a dependency.
sources_read: WebSearch: "Another Virtue of Wavelet Forests" (snippets of arXiv 2308.07809 only; also surfaced arXiv 2604.11338 'Wavelet Forests Revisited')
